note: Synthesises more than 250 studies of model behaviour, which gives an audit a documented basis for saying which capabilities are input-sensitive rather than reliable.
title: Language Model Behavior: A Comprehensive Survey

reading.body:
A survey of more than 250 studies finds that language model abilities are input-sensitive rather than reliable, so capability should not be assumed from model size alone.

The pattern is consistent across the reviewed work. Models handle grammar, meaning, social context, facts, and reasoning at a basic level, but performance shifts with the exact wording and surface details of the input. Scaling to very large sizes improves the quality of generated text without removing false facts, common-sense errors, repetition of training text, or bias toward social groups. The authors attribute many of these failures to learned patterns applied too broadly or too narrowly.

For AI systems, this matters because capability claims are often made at the level of the model rather than the specific input. A model that reasons correctly on one phrasing can fail on a paraphrase of the same question. That makes evaluation a property of the deployment, not the checkpoint, and it argues for testing on the inputs a system will actually receive before high-stakes use.

The data covers English language models before task-specific adaptation, and it is a synthesis of published studies rather than new measurement. It does not report compute, energy, or infrastructure, so it says nothing directly about the grid or the cost of scaling. It also does not quantify how much performance varies by input, only that variation exists across the reviewed literature.

explain_beginner: This survey looks at over 250 studies of how English language models behave before they are adapted for specific tasks. It finds these models can handle basic language skills, such as grammar, meaning, social context, facts, and reasoning, but their performance changes with the exact wording and surface details of the input. Even as models grow to very large sizes and produce better text, they still make factual mistakes, mistakes about everyday situations, repeat text stored from training, and show biases toward social groups. Many problems come from learning patterns too broadly or too narrowly. This matters because it shows their abilities are not always dependable.
explain_business: This survey combines over 250 studies of English language models before they are tailored to tasks. It says these models can do basic language, knowledge, and reasoning work, but their output shifts with exact wording and surface details. Bigger models write better text, yet they still give false facts, make mistakes about common sense, repeat text from training, and show biases toward social groups. Many failures come from applying learned patterns too widely or too narrowly. For executives, this means model abilities should not be treated as reliable by default. It informs decisions about testing, human review, and limiting high stakes use until behavior is checked for the intended inputs.
explain_practitioner: This survey reviews over 250 studies of how English language models act before they are tuned for specific tasks. It reports that models have basic abilities in grammar, meaning, social use, facts, and reasoning, yet those abilities depend on particular inputs and superficial features. Making models much larger improves the quality of their writing, but they still give false information, make mistakes about common sense, repeat text from training, and show biases toward social groups. The authors describe many weaknesses as learned patterns applied too widely or too narrowly. The result is a synthesis of what is known about large language model capabilities, useful for applied work and nearby research.
